en: Now begins the Kaśyapa-smṛti, concerning the description of expiations;
now we shall explain the duties of the householder according to the tradition of Kaśyapa.

One who has established the sacred fires, is devoted to his own wife, maintains the domestic fire and performs the Agnihotra sacrifice, approaches his wife after her ritual bath during her fertile period, and regularly practices the five great sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman; who feeds one, two, three, or four Brāhmaṇas, is intent on vows, observances, burnt offerings, and recitation, is devoted to his mother and father, supports his wife and children, eats only what remains after their needs, observes fasts, avoids the food of those of the three higher castes who have performed a funeral or are in a state of impurity, and subsists by means other than a plough.
And in that regard, there is no unrighteousness in the removal of earth and water or in the cutting down of trees.
For the destruction of wells, bridges, tanks, Brahmins, or temples, one should announce the matter to the Brahmins and offer four oblations.

With the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," this is the first; with "mā nastoke," the second; with "svavāsāḥ," the third; and with "daṃṣṭrābhyām," the fourth—one should cause [the victim] to be released from the pain of the arrow, and one should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to that very deity.
Now, some say that when injury is inflicted upon a cow, a bull, a buffalo, a draught-animal, a sheep, or a goat, the penance depends on whether the act was intentional or unintentional.

For those engaged in milking cows, taming them, overturning them, striking them with stones, using bells as ornaments, applying medicinal oils, or administering the three types of medicinal herbs and remedies, if they fail to achieve their desired goal, they should inform the Brahmins of the transgression, undergo a shaving of the head including the hair, and perform the Prājāpatya penance.
At the conclusion of the observance, one should give a cow.
"An oil-cow and a water-cow," said Kāśyapa.
Now, for the killing of deer, buffalo, gaṇḍuka, boar, śarabha, bear, lion, tiger, frog, pig, fish, crocodile, porpoise, and so forth, there is a fast of one day and night.
At the conclusion of the observance, one should give a cow.
Having performed that three-night rite, he should give gold at its conclusion.

Now, upon killing a crow, a water-hen, a swan, a crane, a kāraṇḍava duck, a ruddy goose, a vulture, a hawk, a wagtail, a lapwing, an owl, a parrot, a myna-bird, a peacock, a kākamadra, a sparrow, a pigeon, a francolin, or others, one should give sesame seeds at the conclusion of a day and night of observance.

Now, therefore, for the killing of a dog, a jackal, a cat, a bull, a hyena, a donkey, a camel, or a Śūdra, one should announce it to the Brāhmaṇas and perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance for three nights as an expiation.
At the conclusion of the performance, one should give offerings of rice along with all its husks.
For killing a chameleon, a snake, a mongoose, a cat, a cow, or a goat, one should observe the penance for three nights; at its conclusion, one should give iron as a gift.
For eating the leavings of those for whose killing an expiation has been prescribed, one shall become pure by performing a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consuming clarified butter.
Upon the birth or death of a child, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after ten nights, a Kṣatriya after fifteen, a Vaiśya after twenty, and a Śūdra after a month.
If this [water] falls within the inner apartments, one becomes pure by bathing on that same day.
One who is not a Brahmin is not born [into that state]; he shall not study, nor cause others to study; he shall neither give gifts nor accept them.
On that day, it was impure for both bipeds and quadrupeds.

Now, for those who have died by fasting, or been struck by lightning, or entered the fire, or died by leaping from a precipice, in battle, or while crossing water, as well as for those stillborn, purification is said to occur after three nights.

Now, regarding the eating of garlic, onions, leeks, mushrooms, and chicken; the drinking of *surā*, *sīdhu*, honey-liquor, and fermented grain-liquor; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; and the initiation (*upanayana*) of one whose *Sāvitrī* has been lost—one should announce these [offenses] to the Brāhmaṇas as requiring expiation. Then, in a place where the sound of village animals or beasts is not heard, having established the fire, swept around it, and strewn grass around it, and having shaved the head including the top-knot (*śikhā*), they deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again according to the previously prescribed rule.
Now the five great sins (mahāpātaka) shall be declared:
a Brāhmaṇa must never be killed by twice-born men, nor should the theft of gold ever be committed. (1)
One should not approach a woman of beautiful form, nor should one engage in physical contact with them;
these are designated by the wise as being known as the great sins (mahāpātaka). ||2||
For the sake of purification, a man should perform the Kṛcchra penance for three years,
or he should give gold equal to his own weight, thereby bringing satisfaction to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having killed a pregnant Ātreyī woman, or a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, one should perform this very same penance.
Now, about to explain the *ākāli* [rites], he says:

"In the case of a sudden, unseasonable thunderbolt strike, an earthquake, or a sudden upheaval of the ground, one should announce the matter to the Brāhmaṇas and offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks made of *samī* wood, smeared with honey, curd, and clarified butter."
"Śanno devī," says Kāśyapa.
In whichever house an owl alights.
A house-lizard or a pigeon enters the house.
Like a hawk or a falcon drawn by a lure, he swoops down like one seeking the prey of a chariot.
They place lamps in their anthill-houses before them.

In the case of the falling out of a door-bolt or the falling out of the bell from a door, one should announce the expiation to the Brāhmaṇas and offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks made of *śamī* wood, smeared with curds, honey, and clarified butter, while reciting the verse "vāstoṣpate" (Kāśyapa).

Now we shall explain the portents: upon the breaking of a vessel of milk, its churning, or its being shattered; upon the falling of a *purohala*, a plough, a yoke, a wheel, or a sacrificial post (*tūpa*); upon the overturning of a chariot, the breaking of a horse, or touching a horse during its menses; upon the setting of the sun, the sight of a storm, lightning, or a bad dream; upon the falling out of an ear or hair, or the falling of a *purohala*; upon touching the site of a sacrificial post (*yūpasthala*), or eating at a house where there is death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) or birth-impurity (*sūtaka*); in these cases, having informed the Brāhmaṇas and having performed an ablution with one's clothes on, one should mutter the *Svapratiratha* hymn—so says Kāśyapa.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the purification of vessels: for a wooden vessel, purification is by scraping; for a leaf-vessel, by ashes; for bronze, lead, tin, and iron, purification is by means of sand.
The grinding of ivory, conch shells, gems, silver, and gold.
Furthermore, earthen objects are to be burned.
For large quantities of grain and cloth, sprinkling is prescribed; for wood, rope, bark, leather, rags, bamboo, split cane, leaves, and foliage, the purification is as for food.

Now we shall explain the marks of those who have previously committed evil deeds: one who has approached a woman who should not be approached becomes afflicted with skin disease; therefore, for the sake of purification of the self according to the Vedas, one must perform penance.
One should exclude these from the śrāddha, as well as any others who defile the row of diners.

They do not eat the food of a *kṣattṛ*, a water-carrier, a dancer, an actor, a wandering mendicant, a charcoal-burner, a temple-attendant, one who lives by the stars, a village priest, one for whom a sacrifice has been performed on his behalf, a bearer of burdens, a *viviṃdaka*, or one born of a remarried woman.
Some who have not yet tamed themselves do not eat.

For one who is conquered by his wife, [the offenses] against village and city priests, those who strike without provocation, those with missing limbs, and those who predict the positions of the stars; |||
These two types of Brahmins should always be avoided during the performance of Śrāddha rites;
for all religious acts depend upon one's wife, and the wife is the means to attain heaven.
Thus has been declared by Brahmā this instruction of Kaśyapa:
seven types of women born again [as daughters] are to be avoided as the lowest of their families. ||5||

She who has been given by word, she who has been given by thought, she for whom the auspicious marriage-thread has been tied, she who has touched the water, and she who has taken the hand in marriage. ||6||
She who has gone to the fire-ritual, and she who is a proponent of external doctrines—
these, as proclaimed by Kaśyapa, shall consume the family like a fire.
Taking up fire, the great multitude of trees sprouts forth;
however, his own lineage, consisting of rebirth and so on, does not sprout again.
Whether it be a father, a brother, a mother, or anyone else—listen to the destination that men who have committed sins reach. (9)
Just as a hawk returning to its nest flies directly to the abode of Yama, so too does a girl who causes death go to hell. (10)
Furthermore, the woman regains her own self within herself, having pierced through the bone alone, as well as the skin, semen, vital energy, and strength. ||11||
Those who, deluded by greed, do not give their daughter in marriage, their entire lineage up to the seventh generation indeed goes to a terrible hell. ||12||
Because going and coming are impossible, it is ordained thus regarding the semen;
having understood this, one should obtain a suitable maiden from that family. (13)
A female slave may be employed for both divine and ancestral rites when she has been acquired through accumulation;
however, a slave purchased by purchase is not ordained as a wife. (14)
A person who gives [a cow] adorned with sacrificial formulas (homa-mantras) obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭomas and Atirātras multiplied a hundredfold. ||15||
But he who, through falsehood and unrighteousness, hands over his daughter to her father, attains a place after death such as that of Dakṣa Prajāpati. ||16||
Thus ends the sublime treatise on Dharma composed by Kāśyapa.
